what_it_does: Mineral UV filter that helps protect skin by blocking and scattering sunlight.
summary_short: Zinc oxide is best known in skincare as a mineral sunscreen filter. It provides broad UV protection and is often chosen for sensitive-skin formulas, though nanoparticle safety depends on exposure route and concentration.
summary_long:
Zinc oxide is a mineral ingredient most commonly used in skincare as a sunscreen filter. On skin, it works by sitting on the surface and helping reduce UV exposure through light scattering, reflection, and absorption. It is also used in some barrier-style skin products because zinc-containing compounds can be soothing and protective.

The strongest skincare-relevant use is photoprotection. The provided research focuses heavily on zinc oxide nanoparticles rather than finished sunscreen performance, but it supports that zinc oxide nanomaterials are widely used because they are stable, low cost, and multifunctional [PMID:unknown].

Nano-sized zinc oxide can make mineral sunscreens feel lighter and look less white on the skin. Safety depends on how the material is used: reviews note that zinc oxide nanoparticles can cause oxidative stress in some test systems, especially at higher exposures, with zinc ions playing a role in cytotoxicity [PMID:unknown]. This does not automatically mean a finished topical sunscreen is unsafe, but it explains why particle size, coating, dose, and formulation matter.

For consumers, zinc oxide is often paired with other sunscreen filters, film-formers, emollients, and pigments to improve spread, wear, and appearance. It is especially common in mineral or hybrid sunscreens. It may leave a white cast, particularly in untinted formulas or on deeper skin tones.

There are no major skincare ingredient conflicts to avoid in routine use. The main practical issues are cosmetic feel, white cast, and making sure the sunscreen is applied generously and reapplied as directed.
